The Failed Taiwan Move and Hsu Hsiu-hsien's "Three Visits" in 1985

In 1982, I was already at the "last hurrah" phase of my TI career (Chapter 11). If my whole TI career had been, like my year at Harvard, a "portable feast," then by 1982 that feast had reached the stage of dirty dishes and scattered crumbs, with the host repeatedly yawning — only I, the guest, was still holding forth. The feast was ending; my departure from TI was only a matter of time. But timing mattered: I still had unvested stock options, and I would need the money from those options to sustain what might be decades of low-income or no-income life ahead.

Of course Premier Sun had promised I "wouldn't suffer a loss" on compensation — but how long would that promise hold? My TI salary was vastly higher than an ITRI President's could ever be. Though Premier Sun was sincere, he wouldn't be Premier forever. Would a new Premier honor the commitment?

There was one solution — if TI agreed: a leave of absence. I could work in Taiwan while technically remaining at TI, drawing no salary but retaining my unvested stock options until they vested, at which point I would exercise them and formally resign. But this required TI's consent.

After returning to Dallas, I asked Barr about a TI leave of absence. I told him frankly that I wanted to work in Taiwan but hoped to retain my stock options. Barr said he would ask Shepherd. A week later, Barr replied: "No! We want to keep you."

On May 4, I wrote to Premier Sun, copying Minister Li and President Fang, laying out my predicament honestly: I wanted to come to Taiwan, but forfeiting my stock options would mean an enormous financial loss (I even told him the likely amount), and my leave-of-absence request had been denied.

Premier Sun and Minister Li each replied over a month later, both expressing disappointment. Minister Li proposed an alternative: I could visit Taiwan a few times a year, one to two weeks each time.

Given how unhappy Shepherd had been last time Minister Li requested "borrowing" me, and knowing Shepherd and Barr's temperaments well, I did not believe they would agree to Minister Li's compromise, so I didn't raise it with them.

On October 31, 1983, my stock options having vested, I resigned from TI. The first thing that came to mind was Taiwan. The day after resigning, I called Minister Li to tell him I was a "free man." Surprisingly, nothing followed the call. Within days, several headhunters had already approached me, so I stopped pursuing Taiwan. Why Minister Li was cold on this occasion remains a mystery to me to this day. But in 1985, after Hsu Hsiu-hsien approached me, Minister Li once again warmly urged me to become ITRI President. And after I took that post, he passionately urged me to found TSMC.

It's just that the one who came to New York in 1985 to recruit me as ITRI President was not the familiar K.T. Li, but the less familiar Hsu Hsiu-hsien.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
Stock options / 股票承购权—允许持有人在特定期间内以预定价格购买公司股票的权利；这是美国科技公司高管薪酬的关键组成部分，也是张忠谋离开德仪时必须精算的财务因素。
Leave of absence (留职停薪)—员工暂时离开职位但保留雇佣关系的安排；德仪拒绝张忠谋的留职停薪请求，等于切断了他在台美之间的退路。

徐贤修「三顾茅庐」（一九八五年，五十四岁）

徐贤修先生曾任美国普渡大学（Purdue University）数学教授，在美国退休后，历任台湾清华大学校长、国科会主委等职；在国科会任内，他建议设立新竹科学工业园区，为当时行政院院长蒋经国采纳。

我在一九八一及八二年来访台湾时，曾拜访国科会主委徐贤修。一九八五年，徐已卸任国科会，接任工研院董事长。工研院院长方贤齐因年龄及健康关系有退休意，徐正在找一个新的院长。

根据徐贤修后来告诉我，他的朋友萨支唐教授在报纸上看到我辞职通用器材公司的消息，就打电话给他推荐我（后来李政委告诉我科技顾问赛驰 Frederick Seitz、RAT Bob Evans 亦在报纸上看到我辞职消息后对李推荐我，但李因为工研院不属他管，所以没有主动找我）。

四月八日，我从通用器材辞职后不到十天，徐贤修就打电话到我的通用器材办公室（我与通用约定辞职后仍可继续用办公室数月），说要和我谈工研院院长事，并约定四月二十八日见面。徐先生很喜欢用中文典故，后来在我工研院院长就职典礼上，他曾说为请我曾「三顾茅庐」；其实他只来过两次，而且我住在川普大厦楼上，与当时地产巨富、后来美国总统的川普上下为邻，我的住所绝对不能说是「茅庐」。

四月二十八日，我与徐贤修谈了两、三小时，我答应五月先到台湾工研院「看看」。五月十四日行政院科技顾问艾凡斯也来纽约看我。艾凡斯是旧识，他任IBM副总裁时，我在德仪，他是我的客户。后来他离开IBM，做创业投资，现来纽约劝我接受工研院职。他说我若做工研院院长，实质上会是「台湾科技长」。当时我不知道他说得对不对，后来做了工研院院长后，才知道艾凡斯此话荒谬之极。台湾没有「科技长」，即使有，也不会是工研院院长。

ReadShift 双语翻译

Hsu Hsiu-hsien's "Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage" (1985, age 54)

Mr. Hsu Hsiu-hsien had served as a mathematics professor at Purdue University in the United States. After retiring from the U.S., he held successive positions as President of Tsing Hua University in Taiwan and Minister of the National Science Council. During his NSC tenure, he proposed the establishment of the Hsinchu Science Park, which was adopted by then-Premier Chiang Ching-kuo.

During my 1981 and 1982 visits to Taiwan, I had called on Minister Hsu. By 1985, Hsu had left the NSC and become Chairman of ITRI. ITRI President Fang Xianqi wished to retire due to age and health, and Hsu was searching for a new president.

According to what Hsu later told me, his professor friend Sah Chi-tang had seen news of my resignation from General Instruments in the newspaper and called to recommend me. (Minister Li later told me that technology advisor Frederick Seitz and RAT Bob Evans had also seen the news and recommended me to Li, but since ITRI was not under Li's purview, Li did not take the initiative to contact me.)

On April 8 — less than ten days after my GI resignation — Hsu called my GI office (GI had agreed I could keep using the office for several months after resigning) to discuss the ITRI presidency, scheduling a meeting for April 28. Mr. Hsu was fond of Chinese literary allusions. At my ITRI inauguration, he would later say he had paid "three visits to the thatched cottage" to recruit me. In truth, he only came twice, and I lived in the Trump Tower, a high-rise luxury building — my residence could hardly be called a "thatched cottage."

On April 28, Hsu and I talked for two to three hours. I agreed to visit ITRI in May first to "take a look." On May 14, Executive Yuan technology advisor Bob Evans also came to New York to see me. Evans was an old acquaintance — when he was IBM Vice President and I was at TI, he had been my client. After leaving IBM for venture capital, he now came to New York to persuade me to accept the ITRI post. He said that if I became ITRI President, I would effectively be Taiwan's "Technology Czar." I didn't know then whether he was right. Only after becoming ITRI President did I realize how absurd Evans' statement was. Taiwan had no "Technology Czar," and even if it did, it wouldn't be the ITRI President.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
"Three visits to the thatched cottage" (三顾茅庐)—三国典故，刘备三次亲往草庐请诸葛亮出山；徐贤修以此自比，但张忠谋幽默指出——他只来了两次，而且张的住所是川普大厦，绝非「茅庐」。
Hsinchu Science Park (新竹科学工业园区)—台湾第一个科学工业园区，成立于一九八〇年；徐贤修在国科会任内推动设立，后来成为全球半导体产业的重要聚落。
Technology Czar (科技长)—对一国科技政策最高主管的俗称；艾凡斯称张忠谋做工研院院长会成为「台湾科技长」，但张认为此言荒谬——工研院院长并无政策制定权。

五月台湾访问与七月决定

五月，我实践对徐贤修的答应，到台湾访问共十一天。在一九八一、八二年两次访问台湾时，我对工研院已稍有了解。这次，听了副院长（胡定华）以及各所（工研院当时共五所）所长的详细报告；十一天内，与徐贤修每天见面，与行政院院长俞国华见面两次，与李国鼎也见面好几次。

除了鼓励我接受工研院院长职，李国鼎重提他三年前（一九八二年）对我提过的创投基金，这三年，他的创投计划已有稍进展，他与在Hambrecht & Quist（H&Q）任职的徐大麟君谈在台湾设创投，于是李国鼎又重萌我亦可在创投扮演一个角色的念头，并且立刻介绍那时也在台湾的徐大麟给我，希望我和徐大麟可以合作。

十一天访问结束时，我是否接受工研院院长职尚无结论。我的条件是：我不计较待遇，可以接受任何俞院长及徐董事长认为合理的待遇，但我只答应「半时」工作，因为我要保留另一半时给李国鼎的创投，或其他在美国的工作（例如天使投资人）。

六月二十四日，徐贤修来纽约访我，告诉我俞院长已答应我的条件，只要我承诺：（一）不要对外说我只是半时；（二）创投与工研院应分开。徐也告诉我俞院长开出来的薪资。如考虑「半时」工作，这薪资相当合理。

六月二十六、七日，我去了旧金山访问H&Q的负责人，询问他们「台湾创投基金」的详细，结果是：「台湾创投基金」无论规模及我与徐大麟君的附带利益，都相当使我失望；更有甚者，徐大麟君本来预备独自经营「台湾创投基金」，现在如果要和我一起经营，而且分享「附带利益」，明显有点失望。所以李政委要我在创投扮演一个角色的主意，并不实际。

纽约的春天快快地过去，现在已到七月，我也已「沉潜」了三个多月。几乎整个七月，我陷入「此后做什么事」的沉思中。经济方面我已无后顾之忧，最重要的考量是：来的工作是否具足够挑战性，能使我再度振作；比较次要，但仍很重要的考量是工作地点和环境。我能否适应？

美国，尤其纽约、德克萨斯、或硅谷，是我最能适应的地点。但挑战性工作机会？在一九八五年七月看来，恐怕只有创业投资（如一九八四年，见第十三章）或继续做「经营顾问」及天使投资人。

台湾呢？无论工作或居住环境，对我都很陌生。但工研院职位看来颇具挑战性。至于徐贤修和俞院长对我「半时」的应承，明显地非常勉强；况且我原本要求「半时」的原意——参加李国鼎的「台湾创投基金」以及终结现存的「经营顾问」及天使投资人工作——一半已不存在（我已发现李政委对我参加「台湾创投基金」的期望并不实际）。我只要结束在纽约的工作（大约一年内）就可以全时在台湾；即使未来一年，也可以至少「四分之三时」在台湾。

七月二十四日，我决定了，我打电话给徐贤修，接受工研院院长职位。

五十四岁，再不闯天下以后也不会了。

ReadShift 双语翻译

The May Taiwan Visit and the July Decision

In May, I kept my promise to Hsu and visited Taiwan for eleven days. During my 1981 and 1982 visits, I had gained some understanding of ITRI. This time, I heard detailed reports from the Vice President (Hu Dinghua) and the directors of each institute (ITRI then had five institutes). Over the eleven days, I met with Hsu daily, saw Premier Yu Guohua twice, and met with Li Guoding several times.

Beyond encouraging me to accept the ITRI presidency, Li Guoding revisited the venture capital fund he had proposed three years earlier (1982). In the intervening years, his VC plans had made some progress — he had discussed setting up a VC fund in Taiwan with Mr. Hsu Ta-lin at Hambrecht & Quist (H&Q). So Li rekindled the idea that I could play a role in the VC fund and immediately introduced me to Hsu Ta-lin, who was also in Taiwan at the time, hoping that Hsu and I could collaborate.

At the end of the eleven-day visit, I had not yet decided whether to accept the ITRI presidency. My terms: I did not care about compensation and would accept whatever Premier Yu and Chairman Hsu deemed reasonable. But I would only agree to work "half-time," because I wanted to reserve the other half for Li Guoding's VC fund or other U.S.-based work (such as angel investing).

On June 24, Hsu came to New York to see me. He told me that Premier Yu had agreed to my conditions, provided I promised: (1) not to tell outsiders I was only half-time; (2) to keep the VC fund separate from ITRI. Hsu also told me the salary Premier Yu was offering. Given the "half-time" arrangement, the compensation was quite reasonable.

On June 26-7, I visited San Francisco to meet with H&Q's principals and inquired about the details of the "Taiwan VC Fund." The result: whether in terms of scale or the carried interest for Hsu Ta-lin and me, the Taiwan VC Fund was deeply disappointing. Worse, Hsu Ta-lin had originally planned to run the fund alone; now having to co-run it and share carried interest with me was clearly unwelcome. So Minister Li's idea of my playing a role in the VC fund was simply impractical.

New York's spring quickly passed; it was now July, and I had been "submerged" in reflection for nearly three months. Throughout most of July, I was lost in contemplation about "what to do next." Financially, I had no worries. The most important consideration: would the work be challenging enough to excite me again? A secondary but still important consideration: the work location and environment. Could I adapt?

The United States — especially New York, Texas, or Silicon Valley — was where I could adapt most easily. But challenging job opportunities? As of July 1985, the options seemed limited to venture capital (as in 1984, see Chapter 13) or continuing as a "management consultant" and angel investor.

Taiwan? Both the work and living environment were quite foreign to me. But the ITRI position seemed genuinely challenging. As for Hsu and Premier Yu's accommodation of my "half-time" request, it was clearly reluctant. Moreover, the original rationale for "half-time" — participating in Li Guoding's "Taiwan VC Fund" while winding down my "management consulting" and angel investing — was half gone (I had realized that Minister Li's expectations about my VC involvement were unrealistic). I could go full-time in Taiwan within about a year of winding down my New York work; even during that year, I could spend at least "three-quarters time" in Taiwan.

On July 24, I decided. I called Hsu Hsiu-hsien and accepted the ITRI presidency.

Fifty-four years old — if I didn't venture forth now, I never would.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
Carried interest (附带利益/绩效分成)—创投基金中普通合伙人（GP）从基金利润中分得的报酬，通常为利润的20%；这是创投行业最核心的利益激励机制。
Angel investor (天使投资人)—以个人资金投资初创公司的早期投资者；张忠谋在离开通用器材后短暂从事天使投资，这是他接触初创企业生态的起点。
"If I didn't venture forth now, I never would" (再不闯天下以后也不会了)—张忠谋在五十四岁做出重大职业转折时的自我激励；放弃美国优渥生活、赴陌生台湾，是他人生中最关键的一次「闯」。
章节

台積電篇一第十五章

张忠谋

台积电篇一·第十五章｜工研院院长（一九八五－一九八八）

工研院的背景

工研院成立于一九七三年，是当时经济部长孙运璿先生的创造物。孙部长有工程背景，是近几十年来台湾政界中最重视科技发展的政要。一九七三年时，孙部长认为政府应该设立一个工业技术研究机构，但公教人员的薪资不足以吸引能干的研究人员，所以他花了不少时间精力，说服立法院通过「工业技术研究院设置条例」，以财团法人形式成立了「工研院」。

「工业技术研究院设置条例」等于是工研院的「宪法」，我现把它纲要如下：

为加速发展工业技术，特设工业技术研究院。本院为财团法人。

本院主管机关为经济部。

本院置董事十一至十五人，其中一人为董事长，均由行政院院长遴选。

工研院既是经济部，所以工研院等于是政府机构。政府机构的工作有保障。所以研院员工既有公职的工作保障，又有财团法人优于公职人员的待遇。

ReadShift 双语翻译

The ITRI Background

ITRI was founded in 1973, the creation of then-Minister of Economic Affairs Sun Yun-suan. Minister Sun had an engineering background and was, in recent decades, the political figure in Taiwan who most valued science and technology development. In 1973, Minister Sun believed the government should establish an industrial technology research institution, but civil service salaries were not sufficient to attract capable research staff. So he spent considerable time and energy persuading the Legislative Yuan to pass the "ITRI Establishment Act," creating ITRI in the form of a foundation.

The "ITRI Establishment Act" is essentially ITRI's "constitution." I outline its key provisions:

To accelerate the development of industrial technology, the Industrial Technology Research Institute is hereby established. This Institute is a juridical foundation.

The competent authority of this Institute is the Ministry of Economic Affairs.

This Institute shall have eleven to fifteen directors, one of whom shall be the Chairman, all selected by the Premier.

ITRI being under the Ministry of Economic Affairs made it effectively a government agency. Government jobs had employment security. So ITRI employees enjoyed both the job security of civil servants and the compensation advantages of a foundation over regular government employees.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
ITRI (Industrial Technology Research Institute，工业技术研究院)—台湾最重要的应用研究机构，成立于一九七十三年；工研院是台湾半导体、光电、机械等关键产业的技术摇篮。
Juridical foundation (财团法人)—以财产为基础、经法院登记成立的法人组织；工研院以财团法人形式运作，享有薪资弹性但主管机关仍为经济部。
"Constitution" of ITRI (工研院的「宪法」)—指工研院设置条例，明定了工研院的使命、定位与治理架构；张忠谋以此条例的「加速发展工业技术」为改革依据。

接任第三任院长

我在一九八五年八月十八日自美飞抵台北，当时工研院徐贤修董事长在机场接我。他告诉我当他对工研院董事会报告我已被行政院院长遴聘为院长时，陈履安董事曾强力反对。陈的反对理由是：「台湾人才很多，为什么要在美国找人？」陈当时任国科会主委，并非工研院的「主管机关」，而且徐强调「别的董事都很支持你」，所以虽然我视陈的反对为不祥预兆，但也没太在意。

八月二十日院长交接典礼，我自前任方贤齐院长接过印鉴，正式成为工研院院长。在就职致词中，我说：「工研院为工业界之一员；如何与工业界配合，将是我主要工作。」接任后的几个星期，为了了解工研院的业务，我听每个所的简报（当时工研院有五个所、一个中心）。

一开始在工研院听简报，就发现这是很累的事。简报者似乎认为这是一出他被命令演出的戏。他写剧本、导演、主演；他用心准备、排演、最后演出；他期待的是我的鼓励和喝彩。

我却认为这是他对我的沟通，我要了解他在做什么？有没有困难？我能不能解决他的困难？更重要的，我要了解他为什么做他在做的？做成了对台湾工业界有没有用？

我在德仪和通用无论听或做简报已有二十多年经验。我维持我的一贯风格：听就打断简报发问，因为问题不能累积，如果一开始不打断发问，以后等于白听；而且，在简报结束后，我问几个重要但在简报中没有提到的问题，例如：市场多大？哪家公司有兴趣？怎么移转研究成果等等。

在德仪和通用，一般简报者（包括我自己）都很能应付这类问题；但是一九八五年的工研院，我的作风竟然造成大大的震撼。当时我不知道，打断简报发问被视为「不尊重简报者」；问一些简报中没有提到、甚至简报者想都没想过的问题更被视为不近人情。其实我问这些问题时绝无要简报者出糗的意思；虽然我知道他大概没想过，但我希望我的发问也许可以启发他的思想。后来看，领情的同仁虽然我自己以为只是坦率，但我在听简报时「不尊重」同仁的恶名，在我上任的头几个月就成立了，也是我后来改革失败原因之一。

ReadShift 双语翻译

Assuming the Third Presidency

On August 18, 1985, I flew from the U.S. to Taipei. ITRI Chairman Hsu Hsiu-hsien met me at the airport. He told me that when he reported to the ITRI Board that I had been appointed by the Premier, Director Chen Lian had strongly objected. Chen's objection: "Taiwan has plenty of talent — why look in America?" Chen was then Minister of the National Science Council, not ITRI's "competent authority," and Hsu emphasized that "all the other directors strongly support you." So although I took Chen's opposition as an ill omen, I didn't dwell on it.

On August 20, at the presidential transition ceremony, I received the official seal from my predecessor, President Fang Xianqi, formally becoming ITRI President. In my inaugural address, I said: "ITRI is a member of the industrial community; how to collaborate with industry will be my primary task."

In the first few weeks after taking office, to understand ITRI's operations, I listened to briefings from each institute (ITRI then had five institutes and one center).

From the very first briefings, I found the experience exhausting. The briefers seemed to treat the session as a play they had been ordered to perform. They wrote the script, directed it, and starred in it. They prepared diligently, rehearsed, and finally performed. My encouragement and applause were what they expected.

I, however, saw this as their communication to me. I wanted to understand: What are they doing? Do they have difficulties? Can I solve them? More importantly, I wanted to understand why they were doing what they were doing, and whether it would be useful to Taiwan's industry.

At TI and GI, I had over twenty years of experience both giving and receiving briefings. I maintained my consistent style: interrupt with questions during the briefing, because questions shouldn't accumulate — if you don't interrupt early, the rest is wasted. Moreover, after the briefing, I asked several important questions that hadn't been addressed: How big is the market? Which companies are interested? How will the research results be transferred?

At TI and GI, most briefers (myself included) could handle such questions easily. But at ITRI in 1985, my approach caused an enormous shock. I didn't know then that interrupting a briefing with questions was seen as "disrespecting the briefer." Asking questions that hadn't been addressed — or that the briefer had never even considered — was seen as unreasonable. In truth, I had absolutely no intention of embarrassing the briefer. Though I knew they probably hadn't thought about these questions, I hoped my inquiries might stimulate their thinking. In hindsight, few colleagues appreciated my intent. My reputation for "disrespecting" colleagues during briefings was established within my first few months — and became one of the reasons my reforms later failed.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
Briefing culture clash (简报文化冲突)—张忠谋在美企养成的「打断发问」风格，与工研院「尊重简报者」的文化产生激烈冲突；这是跨文化管理失败的典型案例。
"ITRI is a member of the industrial community" (工研院为工业界之一员)—张忠谋就职演说的核心命题——工研院不应是闭门研究的学术机构，而应服务于工业界；这句话成为他三年改革的指导思想。
Technology transfer (技术移转)—将研究成果从研究机构转移至产业界的过程；张忠谋认为最有效的移转方式不是授权，而是「把人一起移转」——衍生公司。

三大改革

一九八六、八七年是我勤于改革工研院的时期。我同时推动三个改革。

改革一：十年内一半经费来自民间企业

那时工研院的研究计划只有极少数根据工业界需要，绝大多数都在院内各所长领导下拟就，向经济部申请经费。几乎全部经费都由经济部拨给（有一部分名义上来自国营企业，例如中油、台电，但他们受经济部指示，给工研院钱，并没委托工研院做什么事）。

孙运璿先生在任经济部长时，要工研院做IC计划；后来他任行政院长时，又指示工研院做「自动化」研究；但他只给了题目，这两个大计划的细节，仍由电子所和机械所规划，然后经济部同意。

我认为政府经费的专案有必要，但应该做比较长期——五年、十年后台湾工业界用得到的研究。同时工研院应该出去问工业界他们的近期需要，工研院也应该对工业界推销工研院的研究实力——替民营企业做他们需要的研究，但是也要他们出经费。

工研院的确有这研究实力。一九八五年时，工研院有四千多员工，大部分都有理工学士或硕士学位。大的研究所有一千多员工，小的研究所也有几百员工。而且，照我的想法，长期的政府专案与中短期的工业委托应该有互相滋养作用。

我设了数量目标：十年内（一九九六年）一半经费来自民间企业！我的真正目的是要连接工研院和台湾工业，让工研院做台湾工业界需要的研究。我不愁经费。我任院长时，工研院申请政府经费并不难。我只是要连接工研院和台湾工业界的研究需要，而钱（经费）是最有效的连结方式。

我天真地认为我的目的一定会被大家认同，事实却完全相反。无论院内、院外，都没有接受我的想法。在院内，一般同仁的反应是：我们是研究人，不是营销员，也不是生意人，为什么要我们去推销我们的研究？政府官员一般的反应是：好好的政府出钱的研究不做，为什么要去募民间的钱？工业界的反应是：本来就应政府出经费，做出来的成果如果我们要，应该免费给我们。

我的「改革一」在我任院长时没有被接受，后来几十年也鲜有人提起。倒是最近几年，居然有人重提三十年前工研院旧事，认为当时我的想法不无道理。三十余年事过境迁，我当时失败的痛苦，早已麻木了。

ReadShift 双语翻译

The Three Reforms

1986 and 1987 were the years I was most active in reforming ITRI. I simultaneously pushed three reforms.

Reform 1: 50% of Funding from Industry within Ten Years

At that time, very few ITRI research projects were based on industry needs. The vast majority were conceived by the institute directors within ITRI and submitted to the MOEA for funding. Nearly all funding came from the MOEA. (A portion was nominally from state-owned enterprises like CPC and Taipower, but they contributed at the MOEA's direction without commissioning any actual research.)

When Sun Yun-suan was Minister of Economic Affairs, he directed ITRI to undertake the IC program. Later as Premier, he instructed ITRI to pursue "automation" research. But he only provided the topics; the details of both major programs were planned by the Electronics and Mechanical Institutes and then approved by the MOEA.

I believed government-funded projects were necessary, but should focus on longer-term research — work that Taiwan's industry would need five or ten years out. Meanwhile, ITRI should go out and ask industry what their near-term needs were. ITRI should also market its research capabilities to industry — doing research that private companies needed, but having them fund it.

ITRI did have such research capability. In 1985, ITRI had over 4,000 employees, most holding bachelor's or master's degrees in science or engineering. The major institutes had over 1,000 staff; even the smaller ones had several hundred. Moreover, in my view, long-term government projects and short-to-medium-term industrial contracts should have a mutually nourishing relationship.

I set a quantitative target: 50% of funding from private industry within ten years (by 1996)! My true purpose was to connect ITRI with Taiwan's industry, so ITRI would do the research Taiwan's industry needed. I was not worried about funding. During my presidency, ITRI had no difficulty securing government funding. I simply wanted to link ITRI with Taiwan's industrial research needs, and money was the most effective linking mechanism.

I naively assumed my goal would be universally embraced. The truth was the exact opposite. Neither inside nor outside ITRI did anyone accept my idea. Inside, the typical reaction from colleagues was: We are researchers, not salesmen or businessmen — why should we have to market our research? Government officials generally reacted: The government is generously funding your research — why go chasing private money? Industry's reaction: The government should be paying for this. If they produce results we want, they should give them to us for free.

"Reform 1" was not accepted during my presidency, and for decades afterward, few people brought it up. Only in recent years have people revisited the thirty-year-old ITRI episode and conceded that my thinking had some merit. More than thirty years have passed; the pain of that failure has long since numbed.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
Research funding model (研究经费模式)—张忠谋试图将工研院从「政府全额拨款」转向「政府与民间各半」的经费结构；这一改革虽在当时失败，但方向与后来全球研究机构的趋势一致。
Mutually nourishing relationship (互相滋养作用)—长期基础研究与应用开发之间的正向互动——长期研究提供技术储备，短期应用为长期研究提供方向和经费。
"We are researchers, not salesmen" (我们是研究人，不是营销员)—工研院同仁对张忠谋改革的典型反应，体现了研究机构文化与企业需求之间的根本张力。

改革二：衍生公司，把人也移过去

一个研究案的成果大部分都存在研究者的脑袋里，所以最有效的「技术移转」，应该把研究者都移转到要用这技术的公司去。

一谈到移转人，马上触到工研院的敏感神经。如前文所述，工研院是一个高薪、工作有保障的准政府机构；大部分工研人自视为「研究人」，而不是「工业人」。即使他们的研究成果已转移至工业界，他们还是要待在工研院做研究；在他们心目中，工业公司与他们搭不上关系。

但即使这是同仁的心情，在我任院长的三年内，我还是尽力推动衍生公司，因为我认为衍生公司是达成工研院使命——「加速发展工业技术」的最好做法。工研院在我任院长前的十二年，只衍生了一家公司：联华电子公司（联电），转移了三十多名员工；但在我任院长的三年，我促成了五家衍生公司：

- **台积电**——自电子所转移一百多位员工。 - **盟立自动化公司**——自机械所转移一百多位员工，是台湾第一家「自动化」公司。 - **台湾光罩公司**——自电子所转移三十多位员工。 - **长荣超合金**——自材料所转移四位员工。 - **亿威电子**——自电子所转移二十多位员工。

事实上，虽然在徐贤修、俞国华找我做工研院院长时，他们从未提起，我也没有想到做了工研院院长后要衍生一家半导体公司；但在我就任两周后，李政委邀我去他办公室，在那会议中就提出衍生一家半导体公司（后来名为台积电）的可能性。后来的发展又是异常地快，在我院长任内，筹备台积电及成立台积电后的经营几乎占了我一半时间。

多年后看来，衍生这五家公司，尤其台积电，是我工研院院长任内的最大——也许唯一——成就。但在我任内，这个现在很明显的成就却在当时看不出来。

ReadShift 双语翻译

Reform 2: Spin-offs — Transferring People Along with Technology

The results of a research project reside mostly in the researchers' heads, so the most effective "technology transfer" is to transfer the researchers themselves to the company that will use the technology.

The moment you talk about transferring people, you touch ITRI's raw nerve. As noted earlier, ITRI was a high-paying, secure quasi-government agency. Most ITRI people considered themselves "researchers," not "industrialists." Even when their research results had been transferred to industry, they wanted to stay at ITRI doing research. In their minds, industrial companies had nothing to do with them.

But even if this was the prevailing sentiment, during my three-year presidency I still pushed for spin-offs, because I believed spin-offs were the best way to fulfill ITRI's mission: "to accelerate the development of industrial technology." In the twelve years before my presidency, ITRI had spun off only one company: United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC), transferring about thirty employees. But during my three-year presidency, I facilitated five spin-offs:

• TSMC — over 100 employees transferred from the Electronics Institute.

• Mitel Automation — over 100 employees from the Mechanical Institute; Taiwan's first "automation" company.

• Taiwan Mask Corporation — over 30 employees from the Electronics Institute.

• Ever Superalloy — four employees from the Materials Institute.

• EW Electronics — over 20 employees from the Electronics Institute.

In fact, although neither Hsu Hsiu-hsien nor Premier Yu had ever mentioned it when recruiting me, nor had I considered it myself, that becoming ITRI President would mean spinning off a semiconductor company — just two weeks after taking office, Minister Li invited me to his office and proposed the possibility of spinning off a semiconductor company (later named TSMC). Subsequent developments came with unusual speed. During my presidency, preparing for TSMC's founding and managing its early operations consumed nearly half my time.

Viewed years later, spinning off these five companies — especially TSMC — was the greatest, perhaps the only, achievement of my ITRI presidency. But during my tenure, this now-obvious achievement was far from apparent at the time.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
Spin-off (衍生公司)—由母机构分离出去、独立运营的新公司；张忠谋认为衍生公司是技术移转最有效的方式——因为技术存在于研究者的头脑中。
TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company，台湾积体电路制造公司)—全球第一家专业晶圆代工厂，成立于一九八七年；台积电的诞生彻底改变了半导体产业的分工模式。
Quasi-government agency (准政府机构)—具有政府机构的稳定性和保障，但有一定弹性的组织型态；工研院的「准政府」性格既是优势（稳定揽才），也是改革阻力。

改革三：每年考绩最低三%员工留职察看

我到工研院时，工研院已每年打员工考绩，但考绩的作用不大，仅是少许加薪的差别。不曾有员工因考绩差而被解雇，甚至连正式警告的机制都没有。

考绩制度目的是借「赏罚分明」，而激励成效好的人员，并且警告成效不好的人员。在美国企业内，赏罚幅度可以相当大。举大公司GE为例，威尔许（Jack Welch）在一九八一年任GE总裁后，规定GE每年解雇考绩最差的一〇%。威尔许一直以此政策为傲，是他退休时最成功政策之一。再举德仪为例，每年新年假后的第一个星期，「经营委员会」花整整一个星期的时间，排列公司考绩最佳的前一百名，以及检讨如何处理考绩最差者。

一九八五年工研院的考绩制度，只拷贝了美国企业考绩制度的皮毛，并没有达到借「赏罚分明」而激励或警告同仁的目的。

当然我也知道工研院是一个准政府机构，「赏」的幅度不大（只是多加一点薪，没有分红，更没有股票承购权之类的「奖励」），所以「罚」的幅度也不宜太大。但对考绩最差的少数员工，应该给他们一个正式警告——留职察看半年，不加薪，但也不扣薪，看半年后再说。

有些员工其实有能力可以做好工作，但因为不够努力，所以对这类员工，半年的「留职察看」正可鼓励他们努力一点。有些因为被放在错的位置上，没有能力做这位置的工作，所以对这类员工，半年「留职察看」也可以让上层主管或人力资源单位调动他们到比较适宜的职位。

我并不想解雇任何员工，我只想整顿一下最劣考绩的员工——激励他们努力一点，或转调他们到比较适合他们能力的职位，因而提高工研院的一般表现。

一九八六年，我与徐贤修董事长、副院长、所长、协理们讨论了我的想法后，决定列考绩最低的三%为「留职察看」。徐董事长非常赞成此举，副院长及所长们有几个赞成、有几个有保留。我起初想列五%为「留职察看」，因为有几位所长认为五%太高，所以改为三%。

我没有想到，虽然我们只列三%员工为「留职察看」，但至少三%的员工感到「唇亡齿寒」？还是本来安逸地寄居在准政府机构的工作保障下，现在发现这个外国来的新院长居然威胁起他们的安全感来？总之，黑函满天飞。工研院董事、经济部，甚至立法委员、监察委员都收到黑函。

我的「改革三」，只做了一年，第二年就做不下去了。

ReadShift 双语翻译

Reform 3: Bottom 3% on Probation Annually

When I arrived at ITRI, annual performance reviews were already in practice, but they had little effect — merely modest differences in salary increases. No employee had ever been fired for poor performance. There wasn't even a formal warning mechanism.

The purpose of a performance review system is to "reward the good and punish the bad" — to motivate high performers and warn underperformers. In American companies, the reward-and-punishment range can be quite large. Take GE as an example: after Jack Welch became CEO in 1981, he mandated that GE fire the bottom 10% of performers annually. Welch was always proud of this policy, citing it as one of his most successful initiatives at retirement. Or take TI: every year in the first week after New Year's, the Operations Committee spent a full week ranking the company's top 100 performers and discussing how to handle the worst performers.

ITRI's 1985 performance review system had copied only the veneer of American corporate practices without achieving the motivational or warning purpose of "rewarding the good and punishing the bad."

Of course I understood that as a quasi-government agency, ITRI's "reward" range was small (just slightly higher pay, no bonuses, no stock options), so the "punishment" range should also be modest. But for the small number of worst performers, they should receive a formal warning — six-month probation with no salary increase but no cut, to be reviewed again after six months.

Some employees had the ability to do good work but lacked effort; for them, six months of probation could motivate them to try harder. Some were in the wrong role, lacking the capability for their position; for them, probation could allow management or HR to reassign them to a more suitable position.

I had no desire to fire anyone. I simply wanted to address the worst performers — either motivate them to improve or reassign them to roles that better matched their abilities, thereby lifting ITRI's overall performance.

In 1986, after discussing my ideas with Chairman Hsu, the Vice President, institute directors, and associate directors, we decided to place the bottom 3% on probation. Chairman Hsu strongly endorsed this; among the Vice President and directors, several supported it, several had reservations. I had initially wanted to set it at 5%, but since several directors felt 5% was too high, we settled on 3%.

What I did not anticipate: although we only placed 3% on probation, at least that 3% felt the threat — or was it that those who had long enjoyed the security of a quasi-government job now found that this foreign-born new president was threatening their safety? In any case, anonymous letters flew everywhere. ITRI directors, the Ministry of Economic Affairs, and even legislators and Control Yuan members all received them.

"Reform 3" lasted only one year; the second year it became impossible to continue.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
Probation (留职察看)—对表现不佳员工给予一定期间的观察，期间不加薪但不扣薪，期满后再评估；这是介于「口头警告」和「解雇」之间的中间处分。
Anonymous letters (黑函)—匿名检举信，常被用于政治或组织内的斗争；张忠谋的改革三引发大量黑函攻击，是台湾公机构改革少见的社会现象。

一九八八年——我任工研院院长最后一年

一九八八年是台湾重要的一年，也是我任工研院院长的第三年、也是最后一年。

一月，蒋经国总统去世，李登辉副总统继任为总统。七月，原国科会主委陈履安替代李达海为经济部部长。陈部长三年前以「台湾有许多人才，为什么去美国找工研院院长？」为由，反对我任工研院院长，当时我不很在意，因为国科会不是工研院的「主管机关」。现在陈任我「主管机关」的部长，对我当然是恶耗。

七月，李国鼎政委退休，转任资政。这位受老蒋总统赏识、又在蒋经国手下忠诚服务的「四朝老臣」，在一九八八年已七十八岁。李政委是政府内最赏识我的一人。他的退休，以及退休前的渐渐失势，当然对我不利。

还有，「三顾茅庐」雇我的徐贤修，在一九八八年也面临退休。

听徐董事长说，李总统常自傲他的科技知识，我也知道在我接任工研院院长前，李登辉还是副总统时，陈履安主委就安排了工研院材料所林垂宙所长，经常对李副总统报告世界科技界动态。所以，当李总统在就任两个月后就宣告他要视察工研院，我倒抱了相当好奇及期待——他真的对促进台湾工业技术这么有兴趣？

在我趋前迎接李总统时，他立刻对我考试：「张院长，最近在某某（国外）科技月刊发表的某某新发现，你知道吗？」我不知道，我的惶恐表情换来他的不屑脸色。

接着是参观，以及简报。李总统没有打断我们的简报（他深知台湾不打断简报的「礼貌」），但在我结束最后的纲要、正想邀请总统去餐厅用午餐时，他忽然说：「慢着。」我停住了。他问：「你们与中央研究院及各大学的研究有什么联系？」假如我是一个先进国家研究机构的院长，而这国家的总统问我跟国家最高研究机关有什么联系，我想我可以侃侃而谈。但这是一九八八年的台湾，我们的工业技术相当落后，我已做了两年半工研院院长，一直努力想把工研院和工业界连接起来，现在李总统问的「联系」，恰是相反方向——无关工业界实际需要的方向。

老实说，当时我不清楚工研院与中央研究院以及各大学有什么联系，因为我不认为有这联系，假如有，有什么重要性。我也不记得怎么回答李总统。总之，对李总统，我的回答一定是很令他窝囊。

政府人事的递易——总统、经济部部长、科技政委、工研院董事长——对工研院院长的位置，其实还是次要。只要看我的前任方贤齐院长，以「无为而治」见称，经历了好几轮政府人事变动，却毫发无损。但我一到工研院，就以「改革者」自命；那么，我的命运，就要看我的「改革」是否成功？以及我「兴波起浪」激发起来的情绪了。

两个答案都是负面的。我的三个改革——「十年内一半经费来自民间企业」和「三%员工留职察看」失败；「衍生公司」只是后来成功，当时却有相当阻力及负面反应。至于改革激起的情绪呢？问题可大了。无论院内、院外，都说我没有「人和」。

ReadShift 双语翻译

1988 — My Final Year as ITRI President

In January, President Chiang Ching-kuo passed away; Vice President Lee Teng-hui succeeded him. In July, former NSC Minister Chen Lian replaced Li Da-hai as Minister of Economic Affairs. Minister Chen had opposed my ITRI appointment three years earlier on the grounds that "Taiwan has plenty of talent — why look in America?" At the time I hadn't taken it seriously, since the NSC was not ITRI's "competent authority." Now Chen was the minister of my "competent authority" — decidedly bad news for me.

Also in July, Minister K.T. Li retired and became a Senior Advisor. This "four-dynasty elder," valued by the elder Chiang and loyally serving under Chiang Ching-kuo, was 78 years old in 1988. Minister Li was the single most appreciative sponsor I had in government. His retirement and gradual loss beforehand of influence were obviously detrimental to me.

Moreover, Hsu Hsiu-hsien — the man who had "paid three visits" to recruit me — also faced retirement in 1988.

Chairman Hsu told me that President Lee often boasted of his scientific knowledge. I also knew that before I became ITRI President, when Lee was still Vice President, Minister Chen had arranged for ITRI Materials Institute Director Lin Chui-chou to brief Vice President Lee regularly on global technology trends. So when President Lee announced his visit to ITRI just two months after taking office, I was genuinely curious and eager — was he truly that interested in advancing Taiwan's industrial technology?

As I stepped forward to greet President Lee, he immediately quizzed me: "President Chang, have you read the recent discovery published in [some foreign] science monthly?" I had not. My visible dismay drew a look of disdain.

Then came the tour and briefings. President Lee did not interrupt our briefings (he well knew Taiwan's norm of "politeness" about not interrupting), but as I finished the summary and was about to invite him to lunch, he suddenly said: "Hold on." I stopped. He asked: "What connections do you have with Academia Sinica and the universities?"

Had I been the head of a research institution in an advanced country, and the president asked about my links with the national academy, I could have talked at length. But this was 1988 Taiwan. Our industrial technology was quite backward. I had spent two and a half years as ITRI President striving to connect ITRI with industry. Now President Lee asked about "connections" in precisely the opposite direction — a direction irrelevant to industry's real needs.

Frankly, I was not clear what connections ITRI had with Academia Sinica and the universities, because I didn't think such connections mattered. If they existed, what was their importance? I don't even remember how I answered. In any case, my answer must have been thoroughly unimpressive to President Lee.

The churn of government personnel was, in the end, secondary to the ITRI presidency itself. Consider my predecessor, President Fang Xianqi, famous for "governing by non-action." He weathered several rounds of government personnel changes without a scratch. But the moment I arrived at ITRI, I cast myself as a "reformer." So my fate would depend on whether my reforms succeeded — and on the emotions I stirred up by "making waves."

Both answers were negative. Two of my three reforms had failed. "Spin-offs" would succeed only later; at the time, they faced considerable resistance and negative reaction. As for the emotions my reforms provoked? Both inside and outside ITRI, people said I lacked "harmony with people."

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
"Making waves" (兴波起浪)—指在组织内引发争议或动荡；张忠触自知自己以「改革者」自命，必然兴波起浪，但低估了浪头的大小。
"Harmony with people" (人和)—中国传统文化中「天时、地利、人和」的「人和」——指人际关系的和谐；在工研院改革中，「人和」成为反对改革的理由。

胡定华的辞职与我的去职

雪上加霜的，是副院长胡定华的辞职。

自从我单枪匹马、自命为「改革者」到工研院那时刻，我就把胡定华当作我最亲近的同僚；那时我知道工研院不多，知道台湾更少，我认胡定华为向导。我的所有「改革」，都先与他讨论；尤其衍生台积电一事，胡和电子所所长史钦泰是我的得力助手。

但在一九八七年四月，胡定华忽然对我说他要交通大学当校长。我当下说：「工研院院长好」，我就说：「我不会做很久，如你留下，那我要走时，我一定推荐你为院长。」他很坦白地说：「『由副扶正』在台湾不太有，而且如果你离开，你也不见得有能力推荐我。」在我成长的企业文化里，如果下属有好的出路要离开，我不会强留他，只会祝福他；因为如果真的把他强留下来，我会认为我欠了他一个债，而且是一个还不尽的债。他总是会想：如果去了那个职位，是否会比留着好。

所以在胡定华怀疑他做工研院院长的机会时，我也不再留他，反而鼓励他去交大当校长。但第二天他就告诉我，交大的事已经被人做了。后来阮大年来当交大校长，来看我，告诉我交大校长本来是胡定华，但俞国华院长认为我在工研院需要胡定华为辅佐，所以变成是他了。阮在告诉我时有点不高兴，好像他只是「第二选择」。所以俞院长的这个决定，得罪了三个人：阮，因为只是「第二选择」；胡，因为使他失去当交大校长的机会；我，因为我虽器重胡定华，但不认为那么需要他，而我的老阁却认为我必须要有他辅佐。

俞院长的苦心，还是没用；他能使胡定华不去交大，但不能使他留在工研院。半年后，胡就告诉我他要去H&Q台湾创投基金徐大麟旗下。这基金就是一九八五年我没有接受、花半时与徐大麟共同经营的基金。我不认为对胡定华，这是一个好机会；我认为这机会还比胡定华仍有可能得到工研院院长职位差。但他去意已坚。他在一九八八年二月正式辞职。

胡定华的辞职，锁定了我欠缺「人和」的名声。紧接着他的辞职，我的两个上司（工研院董事长徐贤修及经济部部长李达海）都告诉我：依院长认为我不善处理人事。不久后任陈履安任经济部部长，我立刻发现要见陈部长，远较以前要见李部长难。李达海部长与我有一个相当「随遇而安」的关系。因为我的「改革」需要他的支持，我常去见他，总只要一、两天前打电话与他秘书约就行。陈部长却需要好几天，甚至一、两星期前约，有时约了后还被他临时更改。有一次，我准时到经济部，在他办公外面的客厅等了半小时后，他匆匆出来，见我在等他，对我说：「啊，我要去楼开会，你跟我一起下去，在楼梯上跟我说话吧。」

ReadShift 双语翻译

Hu Ding-hua's Resignation and My Departure

To add frost to the snow, Vice President Hu Ding-hua resigned.

From the moment I arrived at ITRI, a self-appointed "reformer" riding solo, I had treated Hu Ding-hua as my closest colleague. I knew little about ITRI and even less about Taiwan; I regarded Hu as my guide. I discussed all my reforms with him first. On the TSMC spin-off in particular, Hu and Electronics Director Shi Qin-tai were my key lieutenants.

But in April 1987, Hu suddenly told me he was leaving to become President of Chiao Tung University. I said: "The ITRI presidency is better." I told him: "I won't be here long. If you stay, when I leave I'll recommend you as president." He replied candidly: "Promotion from deputy to president is rare in Taiwan, and even if you leave, you might not have the influence to recommend me."

In the corporate culture I grew up in, if a subordinate has a good opportunity to leave, I wouldn't hold him back — I'd only wish him well. For if I truly held him back, I'd feel I owed him a debt that could never be repaid. He would always wonder whether leaving would have been better.

When Hu questioned his prospects for the ITRI presidency, I didn't hold him back — instead I encouraged him to take the Chiao Tung position. But the next day he told me the Chiao Tung job had gone to someone else. Later, Ruan Da-nian, who became Chiao Tung President, visited me and told me the position was originally meant for Hu, but Premier Yu felt I needed Hu's assistance at ITRI, so it went to Ruan instead. Ruan seemed a bit unhappy telling me this, as if he were merely the "second choice." So Premier Yu's decision offended three people: Ruan, for being the "second choice"; Hu, for losing the Chiao Tung presidency; and me, because although I valued Hu, I didn't think I needed him that much, yet my superior believed I must have his support.

Premier Yu's good intentions were futile. He could prevent Hu from going to Chiao Tung, but he couldn't make him stay at ITRI. Six months later, Hu told me he was leaving to join Hsu Ta-lin's H&Q Taiwan VC fund — the same fund I had declined to co-run back in 1985. I did not think this was a good opportunity for Hu; I thought it worse than his chances of eventually becoming ITRI President. But his mind was made up. He formally resigned in February 1988.

Hu's resignation sealed my reputation for lacking "harmony with people." Shortly after his departure, both my bosses — ITRI Chairman Hsu Hsiu-hsien and Minister of Economic Affairs Li Da-hai — told me that in the Minister's view I was poor at handling personnel matters. Soon after, Chen Lian became Minister of Economic Affairs. I immediately found that seeing Minister Chen was far harder than seeing Minister Li had been. Minister Li and I had a fairly relaxed relationship. Because my reforms needed his support, I often visited him — typically just needing to call his secretary a day or two ahead. Minister Chen required scheduling days, even one to two weeks in advance; sometimes appointments were changed at the last minute. Once I arrived at the MOEA on time. After waiting half an hour in the reception room outside his office, he hurried out, saw me waiting, and said: "Oh, I'm going to a meeting downstairs — come with me and talk to me on the stairs."

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
"Second choice" (第二选择)—指在选拔过程中并非首选的候选人；阮大年得知自己只是交大校长的「第二选择」后的不满，体现了组织任命中的人情考量对个人尊严的影响。
Promotion from deputy to president (由副扶正)—从副职升为正职；胡定华认为在台湾的文化中，「由副扶正」不太常见，这句话反映了他对自身晋升前景的悲观判断。
Lacking "harmony with people" (欠缺人和)—张忠谋被公认为缺乏「人和」——即在组织内维持和谐关系的能力；这是他在工研院改革失败的关键原因。

我辞工研院院长职（一九八八年十一月，五十七岁）

此后，我虽然继续努力，但三年后，我已发现我孤独地在逆水行舟。我的「主管」（行政院长和经济部部长）、工研院同仁，甚至工业界都不在我的阵线上。

这样的处境，为什么还要做下去？我辞职的时间已经到了一九八八年十一月，我口头对陈部长辞工研院院长职。

他点头说：「你可以做董事长。」我默然，我早已熟悉董事长的地位。我知道工研院董事长是无权也不需要做什么事的职位。

陈部长接下去说：「我们要决定下一个院长。应该从内部找，你的所长们有谁？」我开始逐一回答：「电子所史钦泰——」他摇头。「机械所徐佳铭——」他又摇头。「材料所林垂宙——」这次他很快打断我：「那就是林垂宙。」十二月九日，董事长及院长交接典礼。我任院长三年、三个月、又二十天。

经济部次长要和我谈董事长的薪水。他先降低我的期待：「当然董事长的薪水不会像院长那么高。」我回答：「为政府省一点钱吧，我不领工研院董事长薪。」

ReadShift 双语翻译

My Resignation from ITRI (November 1988, age 57)

After that, though I continued to strive, three years later I found myself alone, rowing against the current. My "bosses" (the Premier and the Minister of Economic Affairs), my ITRI colleagues, and even industry were not on my side.

Given such circumstances, why continue? The time for resignation had come. In November 1988, I verbally resigned to Minister Chen.

He nodded and said: "You could become Chairman." I fell silent. I knew the Chairman's position well. I knew the ITRI Chairman was a post with no power and nothing to do.

Minister Chen continued: "We need to decide on the next president. We should look internally — among your institute directors, who would you suggest?"

I began: "Electronics — Shi Qin-tai..." He shook his head. "Mechanical — Xu Jiaming..." He shook his head again. "Materials — Lin Chui-chou..." This time he cut me off quickly: "Then it's Lin Chui-chou."

On December 9, the Chairman and President transition ceremony took place. I had served as President for three years, three months, and twenty days.

The Vice Minister of Economic Affairs wanted to discuss the Chairman's salary. He first lowered my expectations: "Of course the Chairman's salary won't be as high as the President's."

I replied: "Save the government some money — I won't take a chairman's salary from ITRI."

反省

五年内（一九八一—一九八八年，五十二至五十七岁）我辞了三次职。先是德仪，再是通用，现在是工研院。我有严重的挫折感。十几年前四十几岁时纵横全球半导体业的气概，已消失殆尽了。怎么了？难道我真的已走上所谓「彼得原理」的路——一个经理人总是被摆升到他能的位置？一九八八惨的台湾冬天，当工研院旧同事甚至台积电新同事窃窃私语「张忠谋完了」之时，也是我反省之时。

我并不觉得我在工研院的改革方向错误。我认为要有成效，工研院必须紧密连接工业，而工业界委托工研院做研究、而且负担这部分经费是很好的连接方法；我也认为衍生公司是最有效的技术移转，也是最有效的工业连接；我也认为内部人事方面，应该多一点竞争、少一点保护。

那么为什么我的改革失败了？其实答案早就出现了。我错认工研院是我手掌上的黏土，我可随我意志塑造她。事实上，工研院绝对不是我手掌上的黏土，她有独立的性格，她有她「准政府机构」的组织文化。基本上，她认为她活得很好，她只要多点政府经费，她不愿任何改革。

既定了裁、总经理位置，到台湾做事，是没有归路的。「过河卒子」不能退后，只能向前。向前只有一条路：工研院衍生出来的台积电。

ReadShift 双语翻译

Reflection

Within five years (1981–1988, ages 52 to 57), I had resigned three times — first from TI, then GI, now ITRI. I felt severe frustration. The swagger I had possessed a decade earlier, when I strode across the global semiconductor industry in my forties, had evaporated. What happened? Had I truly fallen victim to the "Peter Principle" — that a manager is eventually promoted to his level of incompetence? During the bitter Taiwanese winter of 1989, when old ITRI colleagues and even new TSMC colleagues whispered that "Morris Chang was finished," it was also a time of deep reflection for me.

I did not believe my reform direction at ITRI had been wrong. To be effective, ITRI had to connect closely with industry; having industry commission and fund research was an excellent bonding mechanism. I also believed that spin-offs were the most effective technology transfer and the most effective industrial connection. And I believed that internally, there should be more competition and less protection.

So why had my reforms failed? The answer had been apparent all along. I had mistaken ITRI as clay in my hands, to be molded at my will. In truth, ITRI was emphatically not clay in my hands. She had her own independent character. She had the organizational culture of a "quasi-government agency." Fundamentally, she believed she was doing just fine — she just wanted a bit more government funding and resisted any reform.

Having severed all bridges — leaving behind executive positions at TI and GI — coming to Taiwan was a journey with no return. A "soldier crossing the river" cannot go back; he can only move forward. There was only one road forward: TSMC, the company spun off from ITRI.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
Clay in my hands (手掌上的黏土)—张忠谋反省自己错将工研院视为可按自己意志塑造的材料；这一直觉错误——忽视了组织文化的独立性——是他改革失败的根本原因。
章节

台積電篇一第十六章

张忠谋

台积电篇一·第十六章｜与命运的约会

倡议台积电

「我与命运有一个约会！」（I have a rendezvous with destiny!）这句话，现在不流行了，但在上世纪中期，却常从美国人——尤其年轻美国人口中听到。

在我一生中，也有两次对自己说这话。第一次是一九五八年，我自熟悉的「文化城」波士顿，开四天车到陌生的「牛仔乡」达拉斯，向德州仪器公司报到；第二次是一九八五年，我决定离开已经安身立命的美国，来到人地文化生疏的台湾。

两次与命运赴约都做对了。第一次去德仪赴约，德仪改变了我前半生；第二次去台湾赴约，台湾改变了我后半生。只是，我起初以为台湾的约会地点是工研院，后来命运告诉我我错了——约会地点是台积电。

工研院院长交接典礼的第二天（一九八五年八月二十一日），方前院长就拿了一张纸，对我交代「要办事项」；第一件显然是方前院长最担心的。那就是：三家华裔美商创办的IC设计公司——国善、茂矽、及华智，各要求政府出资为每家建晶圆厂。那时建一座晶圆厂至少需要几千万美元，三座就要一亿美元以上，怎么办？

对这么无理的要求，我的立刻反应是：拒绝他们不就完了？但这答案似乎不能使方前院长释怀。第二天我就找了胡定华副院长及电子所所长史钦泰，问他们为什么不能干脆拒绝这三家IC设计公司的无理要求？是否还有什么「隐情」？

胡、史说没有「隐情」，但有「忧虑」。政府不是已有十年之久，出巨资给工研院研究IC？政府不是要建立台湾IC工业？现在，现成的IC公司要政府资助他们建厂，政府为什么不帮忙？难道政府「促进工业技术发展」的雄心壮志，只限于让工研院研究又研究？

胡与史当然觉得政府不能答应这三家公司建晶圆厂的要求，但也认为不能只说「不」，要给他们一个「交代」。

这一切发生在我出任院长的头几天，而且发生在工研院内经费最大、员工最多、也被认为最成功的研究案上。但是工研院的矛盾已暴露无遗：研究工作可以自以为很成功，但对工业的利益却说不出来。

方贤齐不是唯一担心怎么交代这三家IC设计公司之人。两星期后（九月四日），李国鼎政委要见我。李一开头就提此事。我已有几乎两星期时间想此问题，所以我当时就提「共同晶圆厂」（Common Wafer Fab）观念。李似甚喜我有答案，告诉我他要多召集几个人，一起讨论我的建议。

ReadShift 双语翻译

The Founding of TSMC

"I have a rendezvous with destiny!" This phrase is no longer fashionable, but in the mid-20th century, one often heard it from Americans — especially young ones.

In my own life, I have said these words to myself twice. The first time was in 1958, when I drove four days from the familiar "city of culture" Boston to the unfamiliar "cowboy country" Dallas to report to Texas Instruments. The second time was in 1985, when I decided to leave America — where I had already put down roots — for Taiwan, a land whose people and culture were foreign to me.

Both rendezvous with destiny turned out right. The first, at TI, changed the first half of my life. The second, in Taiwan, would change the second half. Only, I initially assumed the rendezvous point in Taiwan would be ITRI. Later, destiny told me I was wrong — the rendezvous point was TSMC.

The day after the ITRI presidential transition ceremony (August 21, 1985), former President Fang handed me a list of "action items." The first was clearly what worried Fang most: three Chinese-American-founded IC design companies — Mosel, Vitelic, and HMC — each demanded that the government fund a wafer fab for them. At that time, building a single fab cost at least tens of millions of dollars; three fabs would exceed $100 million. What to do?

My immediate reaction to such unreasonable demands: Just say no. But this answer didn't seem to put Fang's mind at ease. The next day I called in Vice President Hu Ding-hua and Electronics Director Shi Qin-tai and asked them: Why not simply refuse these three IC design companies' unreasonable demands? Was there some "hidden story"?

Hu and Shi said there was no "hidden story," but there were "concerns." Hadn't the government spent heavily for ten years funding ITRI's IC research? Wasn't the government trying to build Taiwan's IC industry? Now, actual IC companies were asking the government to help them build fabs — why wouldn't the government help? Was the government's ambition to "promote industrial technology development" limited to letting ITRI do research and more research?

Hu and Shi certainly felt the government couldn't grant these three companies' requests for fabs, but they also felt that simply saying "no" wasn't enough — they needed to give them an "answer."

All this happened in my first few days as president, and it concerned ITRI's largest, most-staffed, and supposedly most successful research program. But ITRI's contradiction was now fully exposed: the research could consider itself very successful, yet could not articulate its benefit to industry.

Fang Xianqi was not the only one worried about how to handle these three IC design companies. Two weeks later (September 4), Minister K.T. Li asked to see me. Li brought up the matter right away. I had spent nearly two weeks thinking about this problem, so I immediately proposed the "Common Wafer Fab" concept. Li seemed delighted that I had an answer and told me he would convene a larger group to discuss my proposal.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
Common Wafer Fab (共同晶圆厂)—张忠谋最初的构想——由政府出资建一座晶圆厂，供多家IC设计公司共享使用；这个概念后来演化为「专业晶圆代工」模式。
IC design company (IC设计公司)—只从事IC设计、不拥有晶圆厂的公司（即「无厂IC设计公司」）；国善、茂矽、华智是台湾最早的一批IC设计公司。

「专业晶圆代工」商业模式

三天后（九月七日，星期六）李政委又开会，这次有谢森中（交通银行董事长）、GRIER（国库署长兼开发基金执行长）及江万龄（中华开发银行总经理）。假使政府同意办新的公司，开发基金是最可能的投资者；交银也是可能的投资者；江万龄在场，我想是因为中华开发曾投资国善，所以江很在意政府如何对国善交代。

在会议中，李政委要我重述一次我三天前对他提的「共同晶圆厂」观念，然后征求谢、张及江的意见。谢和张赞同「共同晶圆厂」，江表示国善仍希望有他们自己的晶圆厂。李政委是一位决定明快、而且没有太多耐心与人辩论的人。他很快嘱咐我准备对俞国华院长简报。

当天下午，李打电话给我：「已约定九月十日（星期二）下午四点半」，他兴奋地对我说，「想不到他（俞院长）那么热心，那么快就答应听你报告。」一九八五年八月二十一日（方贤齐对我讲「要办事项」）至九月四日（我对李国鼎提「共同晶圆厂」）这十四天，可说是我一生中创新价值最高的两周。价值连城的「专业晶圆代工」（Dedicated Foundry）商业模式在此两周诞生。

在这两周，我把我过去二十几年经营半导体业的经验，以及对工研院IC计划的观察和了解，整理、综合起来，达到了一个在当时台湾具备的条件下，最有成功机会的半导体公司商业模式。

当时，世界上几乎所有稍具规模的IC公司都是「垂直整合型」（Integrated Device Manufacturer, IDM），营业范围包含IC设计、晶圆制程研发、晶圆生产、IC营销。这些IDM如有多余产能，也为没有晶圆厂的设计公司（例如在通用器材公司碰到的Chips&Technologies及Atmel）代工。

台湾要成立一家新的IC公司，要从工研院IC案出发，我检验工研院IC案的能力：

- IC设计——能力低。 - 晶圆制程研发——当时（一九八五年）世界最先进的「节点」技术是一微米；工研院还在二微米，落后二代半（一.五微米是一代，一.二五微米是半代），大约三年左右。 - 晶圆生产——工研院「示范线」的良率优异。这是工研院很重要、也是唯一强点。 - 没有在世界市场营销能力。

经过这样的分析，新公司应该具有的商业模式已呼之欲出——只帮客户做晶圆生产，而且目前只能做「成熟节点」技术的生产。当然，新公司必须继续晶圆制程研发，否则制程技术会愈来愈落后；而且希望有朝一日，也能做尖端技术的生产服务。

ReadShift 双语翻译

The "Dedicated Foundry" Business Model

Three days later (September 7, Saturday), Minister Li convened another meeting, this time with Xie Senzhong (Chairman of the Bank of Communications), the Director-General of the National Treasury Agency (also Executive Director of the Development Fund), and Jiang Wanling (General Manager of China Development Bank). If the government agreed to establish a new company, the Development Fund was the most likely investor; the Bank of Communications was also a possible investor. I believe Jiang was present because China Development had invested in Mosel, so Jiang cared how the government would handle Mosel.

At the meeting, Minister Li asked me to restate the "Common Wafer Fab" concept I had presented three days earlier, and then solicited the opinions of Xie, the Director-General, and Jiang. Xie and the Director-General endorsed the Common Wafer Fab. Jiang indicated that Mosel still wanted their own dedicated fab. Minister Li was a man of swift decisions and not much patience for debate. He quickly instructed me to prepare a briefing for Premier Yu.

That afternoon, Li called me: "Scheduled for September 10 (Tuesday) at 4:30 PM," he said excitedly. "I didn't expect him (Premier Yu) to be so enthusiastic and agree so quickly to hear your report."

Those fourteen days — from August 21 (when Fang Xianqi gave me the "action items") to September 4 (when I proposed the "Common Wafer Fab" to Li Guoding) — were perhaps the two most innovative weeks of my life. The priceless "Dedicated Foundry" business model was born in those two weeks.

During those two weeks, I organized and synthesized everything I had learned from over twenty years in the semiconductor industry, together with my observations of ITRI's IC program, to arrive at the business model that offered the highest probability of success given Taiwan's conditions at the time.

Back then, virtually every semiconductor company of any scale in the world was an Integrated Device Manufacturer (IDM), spanning IC design, process R&D, wafer fabrication, and IC marketing. When these IDMs had surplus capacity, they did foundry work for fabless design companies (such as Chips&Technologies and Atmel, which I had encountered at General Instruments).

For Taiwan to create a new IC company based on ITRI's program, I assessed ITRI's capabilities:

• IC design — low capability.

• Process R&D — the world's most advanced "node" in 1985 was 1 micron; ITRI was at 2 microns, two-and-a-half generations behind (1.5 microns is one generation; 1.25 microns is half a generation), roughly three years behind.

• Wafer production — ITRI's "demonstration line" had excellent yield. This was ITRI's most important — and only — strength.

• No capability to market in world markets.

From this analysis, the new company's optimal business model became clear:只做晶圆生产，而且目前只能做「成熟节点」技术的生产。

Of course, the new company would need to pursue process R&D, otherwise its technology would fall further behind. And hopefully, one day it would be able to offer leading-edge technology as well.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
IDM (Integrated Device Manufacturer，垂直整合型制造商)—涵盖设计、制造、销售全流程的半导体公司（如德仪、英特尔）；一九八五年的全球半导体产业几乎全由IDM主导。
Dedicated Foundry (专业晶圆代工厂)—「只制造、不设计」的专业晶圆代工模式——这是张忠谋对半导体产业最重要的商业模式创新。
Node / Process node (节点/制程节点)—指晶圆制造中最小特征尺寸的世代（如1微米、0.5微米）；「节点」的推进是半导体技术进步的核心指标。

初步决定办台积电

这样以自己所长决定自己「商业模式」，却留下一个大的问题：「专业晶圆代工」能有多少生意？对这问题，当时我没有确切答案，但有若干线索；这些线索也使我在构想未来新公司的经营策略上，加了几条要点：

我们的客户将会是刚萌芽的IC设计公司；或是自有晶圆厂但不愿多投资的IDM公司；也可能是大规模、有IC设计能力的电脑公司。总之，作为他们的晶圆代工者，我们与客户站在同一阵线上。所以，「不与客户竞争」，以及「客户是我们的伙伴」也成为新公司的座右铭。

我们的长处是成熟技术的IC生产，我们提供给客户的价值是：让客户相信我们比竞争者（那时的竞争者是IDM）可靠。毕竟竞争者只是以代工为副业，而代工是我们的专业。所以，「对客户不轻易承诺，一旦做出承诺，必定不计代价、全力以赴」成了我们的座右铭。

新公司的市场绝大部分会在美国；次之，欧洲及日本；台湾市场相对地相当小。新公司初期依赖台湾市场，但必须急急开发美国市场。我熟悉美国市场，但我的本职是工研院院长，而且当时是忙碌于改革的工研院院长。所以，新公司的总经理应该是一个有能力为新公司开发美国市场之人——看起来应该有美国半导体公司CEO经验。

李政委在九月七日（星期六）告诉我要我在九月十日下午对俞院长报告「共同晶圆厂」案。次日为星期日，我不想惊动胡定华副院长及史钦泰电子所所长，但星期一早，我就到办公室召集胡、史一起准备对俞院长的报告。忙了一天多，许多投影片还是我的秘书手写的。这份投影片报告现在已在台积电创新馆长期展览。

我以严肃但坦荡的心情面对俞院长及出席的政府首长——政委、经济部部长李达海、经建会主委赵耀东、财政部次长何显重、国科会主委陈履安、行政院秘书长王章清及院、部、会等幕僚共二十余人。我严肃，因为如何继续政府已努力十年的IC计划是一个重要课题；我坦荡，因为我认为我个人利益不牵涉在这课题里，况且我到台湾还不到三星期，此时此刻要对行政院院长报告一个可能新公司的建议，是突如其来的要求。

我知道与会者除李政委及陈主委外，都不太懂IC，即使李、陈基本也是外行，所以尽量「深入浅出」，报告要点摘要如下：

- IC对信息社会及经济的重要性；美、欧、日、韩纷纷巨额投入，世界IC业剧烈竞争状态。 - 台湾自一九七五年开始研究IC，此举很有先见，但IC技术发展甚快，十年来工研院的IC技术非但没有与先进国家缩短距离，反而更落后。 - 台湾IC公司（包括联电、华智、茂矽、国善）均在「临界规模」以下。 - 对台湾而言，IC是一个高代价的长期赌博。是否要进行这个赌博，是一个值得仔细考虑的问题。

如果进行这个赌博，有两条路可走：（一）成立新公司（暂命名为台湾电路制造有限公司），采取「专业晶圆代工」商业模式；（二）增资联电。（一）之优点为「专业代工」，成功机率较大；（二）之优点为可利用现成联电经营团队。

无论（一）或（二），初步营运计划为：（A）租赁工研院「示范线」；（B）开始建新厂，产能每月三万片六吋晶圆；五年内需要投资（包括自有资本及银行贷款）为美元两亿四千三百五十万元。

我讲四十五分钟，接着俞院长要求出席者发表意见约一小时，最后俞院长做结论：「工研院所提成立新公司发展超大型积体电路……其可行性如何？如何筹组？……请李政委约集有关单位研究后再议。」在我提的两个选择中，他已选择了（一）。

ReadShift 双语翻译

The Preliminary Decision to Found TSMC

Designing a business model around our strengths, however, left a big question: How much business would there actually be for a "dedicated foundry"? I had no precise answer, but I had several clues; these clues also led me to add several points to the new company's operating strategy:

Our customers would be nascent IC design companies; or IDMs with fabs but unwilling to invest more; or large computer companies with IC design capability. In any case, as their foundry partner, we would stand on the same side as our customers. Hence, "we do not compete with our customers" and "our customers are our partners" would become the new company's mottos.

Our strength would be mature-technology IC production. The value we offered customers: making them trust us more than competitors (then, IDMs). After all, competitors treated foundry as a sideline; foundry would be our specialty. So "never make promises lightly — once a promise is made, spare no cost and go all out" became another motto.

The new company's market would be overwhelmingly in the U.S., followed by Europe and Japan; the Taiwan market would be relatively tiny. Initially, the new company would depend on Taiwan, but it had to urgently develop the American market. I knew the American market well, but my primary role was ITRI President, and a busy reform-minded one at that. So the new company's General Manager should be someone capable of opening the U.S. market — seemingly, someone with experience as a U.S. semiconductor CEO.

On September 7 (Saturday), Minister Li told me to report on the Common Wafer Fab to Premier Yu on the afternoon of the 10th. The next day being Sunday, I didn't want to bother Vice President Hu or Director Shi, but early Monday morning I called Hu and Shi to my office to prepare the briefing. We worked for more than a day; many slides were handwritten by my secretary. That slide presentation is now on permanent display at the TSMC Innovation Museum.

I faced Premier Yu and the attending government leaders — the Minister, MOEA Minister Li Da-hai, CEPD Chairman Zhao Yaodong, MOF Vice Minister He Xianzhong, NSC Minister Chen Lian, Secretary-General Wang Zhangqing, and over twenty staff from the Yuan and ministries — with a serious but open heart. I was serious because how to continue the government's decade-long IC effort was a vital question. I was open because I had no personal stake in the matter. Moreover, I had been in Taiwan less than three weeks; being asked to present a proposal for a possible new company to the Premier was a sudden demand.

I knew that aside from Minister Li and Minister Chen, most attendees didn't understand ICs. Even Li and Chen were essentially laypeople. So I made it as accessible as possible. The key points:

• The importance of ICs to the information society and economy; the U.S., Europe, Japan, and Korea investing heavily; intense global competition.

• Taiwan had started IC research in 1975, showing foresight, but IC technology had advanced so rapidly that ITRI's technology had not merely failed to close the gap — it had fallen further behind.

• Taiwan's IC companies (including UMC, Vitelic, Mosel, and HMC) were all below "critical mass."

• For Taiwan, IC was a high-stakes, long-term gamble. Whether to take this gamble deserved careful consideration.

If taking the gamble, there were two paths: (1) establish a new company (tentatively named Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company), adopting the "dedicated foundry" business model; (2) increase capital for UMC. Path (1)'s advantage: dedicated foundry, higher probability of success. Path (2)'s advantage: leverage UMC's existing management team.

Either path: (A) lease ITRI's "demonstration line"; (B) begin building a new fab with monthly capacity of 30,000 6-inch wafers; requiring total investment (equity plus bank loans) of $243.5 million USD over five years.

I spoke for 45 minutes. Premier Yu then solicited opinions from attendees for about an hour. Finally, Premier Yu concluded: "Regarding ITRI's proposal to establish a new company for VLSI development... What is its feasibility? How to organize it?... I ask Minister Li to convene relevant units for further study." Of the two options I had presented, he had already selected option (1).

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
"We do not compete with our customers" (不与客户竞争)—台积电最核心的经营原则——只代不设计与客户竞争；这一原则是台积电能够取得IC设计公司信任的基础。
Critical mass (临界规模)—指企业达到能自我维持、具备竞争力的最小规模；张忠谋认为当时台湾所有IC公司都未达临界规模。
High-stakes, long-term gamble (高代价的长期赌博)—张忠谋对IC产业投资本质的形容——投入极大、回收极长、不确定性极高；这也是政府决策者必须面对的现实。

阻力与飞利浦的投资兴趣

当时我的感觉，虽然与会者在会前不太懂IC，但我的「深入浅出」相当成功，至少从他们的发言听来，他们听懂了我的要点。后来我听说李达海部长要他的经济部下属学学我的简报技巧。李部长是前中油董事长，没有IC经验，连他都听懂了，这是我这次简报的一大成就。

李政委此后一星期内开了两次会（九月十三、十七日），最后李政委决定对俞院长建议照我的提议（一）进行台积电，政府出资四八%，其余民间出资。

对台积电的阻力来自国科会陈主委以及他的下属新竹科学园区管理局。

今日台湾怀念孙运璿、李国鼎、赵耀东，认为他们是台湾经济的大功臣。但是在一九八〇年代，陈履安是一个非常有影响力的人物。一九八五年时，陈刚四十八岁，比起李（七十五岁）、赵（六十九岁），他着实是青壮派。他有显赫的家世——外祖父谭延闿曾任大陆时代国民政府主席，父亲陈诚曾任副总统及行政院院长；又有不凡的学歷——台大学士、纽约大学硕士博士；他更有政治企图心，事实上，后来也实现了一部分他的企图心——经济、国防部长，监察院长，以及一九九六年总统候选人。

但是，我始终没有得到他的认可。在他尚未见我面时，他就反对我任工研院院长。在我倡议台积电时，他反对政府投资台积电。这次，我想他的理由是台积电不会成功，政府若投资，投资会泡汤。

他有一个替代方案——新竹科学园区管理局提出的方案。亚利桑那州科学园区建议他们在新竹科学园区建立「洁净室模组」（Clean Room Module），以此应付IC设计公司的要求。要点：台湾不必投资。

这个替代方案也许解决了三家设计公司的要求，但毫不解决更大、台湾已苦心经营十年的IC计划未来。

十月六日，李政委告诉我俞院长听了陈主委反对的话后「很不自在」。李政委拟找国外顾问公司评审我倡议的「专业晶圆代工」商业模式。

陈主委没有放弃亚利桑那州在新竹科学园区盖「洁净室模组」的计划。后来他和李政委各退一步：陈不把他的计划作为台积电的「替代方案」，而说台积电是「大厨房」，他们的计划是「小厨房」，两者可以并立；李也同意两者可以并立。让张忠谋搞台积电，陈及新竹科学园区管理局搞他们的「小厨房」，互不阻挠。再后来，台积电办成了，但「小厨房」却没办成。听说原因是「没有客户」。其实，当时台积电又何尝有客户？我凭借的是我新创的「专业晶圆代工」、「不与客户竞争」模式、工研院「示范线」的优异良率以及对我自己经营能力的信心。

ReadShift 双语翻译

Resistance and Philips' Investment Interest

My sense at the time was that although attendees hadn't understood ICs before the meeting, my "accessible" presentation was quite successful — at least from their comments, they had grasped the key points. I later heard that Minister Li Da-hai asked his MOEA subordinates to study my briefing techniques. Minister Li, former Chairman of CPC with no IC experience, had understood it — this was a major achievement of my presentation.

Minister Li convened twice in the following week (September 13 and 17). Ultimately, he decided to recommend to Premier Yu that they proceed with TSMC per my proposal (1), with the government contributing 48% and private investors the remaining 52%.

Resistance to TSMC came from NSC Minister Chen Lian and his subordinate, the Hsinchu Science Park Administration.

Today, Taiwan remembers Sun Yun-suan, Li Guoding, and Zhao Yaodong as pillars of Taiwan's economic miracle. But in the 1980s, Chen Lian was a highly influential political figure. In 1985, Chen was 48, genuinely younger than Li (75) and Zhao (69). He had illustrious lineage — his maternal grandfather Tan Yankai had served as Chairman of the Nationalist Government on the mainland; his father Chen Cheng had served as Vice President and Premier. He had an impressive academic record — NTU bachelor's, NYU master's and doctorate. And he had political ambition; indeed, he later realized part of it — Minister of Economic Affairs, Minister of Defense, President of the Control Yuan, and 1996 presidential candidate.

But I never won his approval. Before he even met me, he had opposed my ITRI appointment. When I proposed TSMC, he opposed government investment in it. This time, I believe his reasoning was that TSMC would not succeed, and if the government invested, the investment would be lost.

He had an alternative — a proposal from the Hsinchu Science Park Administration. The Arizona Science Park had suggested they build a "Clean Room Module" in Hsinchu Science Park to meet the IC design companies' requirements. Key point: Taiwan wouldn't need to invest.

This alternative might address the three design companies' demands, but it did absolutely nothing to resolve the larger question of Taiwan's decade-long IC program's future.

On October 6, Minister Li told me that Premier Yu had been "quite uncomfortable" after hearing Minister Chen's objections. Minister Li planned to engage a foreign consulting firm to evaluate my "dedicated foundry" business model.

Minister Chen didn't abandon the Arizona "Clean Room Module" plan. Eventually he and Minister Li each gave ground: Chen stopped framing his plan as an "alternative" to TSMC, instead calling TSMC the "big kitchen" and his plan the "small kitchen" — the two could coexist. Li agreed to let the two coexist: let Morris Chang build TSMC, while Chen and the Hsinchu Science Park built their "small kitchen," neither interfering with the other. In the end, TSMC succeeded, but the "small kitchen" never got built. I heard the reason was "no customers." But did TSMC have customers at that time? What I had to rely on was my newly created "dedicated foundry" model, the "we do not compete with customers" principle, ITRI's excellent demonstration-line yields, and confidence in my own operating ability.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
Clean Room Module (洁净室模组)—科学园区提供的标准化洁净室空间，供IC设计公司租用；陈履安的替代方案主张以此代替投资建厂。
Big kitchen vs. small kitchen (大厨房vs小厨房)—陈履安将自己的「洁净室模组」方案与台积电并比喻为「小厨房」与「大厨房」；台积电成了，小厨房却无疾而终。
Foreign consulting firm evaluation (国外顾问公司评审)—陈履安试图借国外顾问公司的权威来否定张忠谋的商业模式；李政委怒斥：「关于半导体问题，国外顾问公司是要请教张忠谋的，哪里有要他们评估张忠谋的道理。」

飞利浦的投资与五人小组

十月初，也就是李政委担心俞院长听了陈主委话后「不自在」之时，荷兰飞利浦公司主动对李政委表示：飞利浦有兴趣投资他们在报章上读到的新IC公司计划。飞利浦是一个多元跨国公司，其中一元是IC，他们也有自主IC技术。所以，如果他们的投资能实现，也就满足了俞院长的筹资要求。

获李政委消息后，我紧锣密鼓进行飞利浦案。我花几天时间写就了对飞利浦的投资建议，交给飞利浦在台湾的技术经理转达飞利浦总部。十一月三日至六日，我亲赴荷兰访问飞利浦在荷兰的两大基地：奈梅亨（Nijmegen）及恩荷芬（Eindhoven）。十一月中旬，飞利浦重申他们的合资兴趣，当然许多条件和细节尚待谈判，而这类谈判往往需要好几个月，但我相信他们有诚意。

十月八日我去见俞院长，俞把李政委的签呈（建议照我意见进行台积电）交给我，要我「再研究」；同时他指示了两点：我们建议的自有资本对贷款比例（五十/五十）不够保守，应该改为七十（自有资本）/三十（贷款）；第二点：经过这样一改，民间投资的需要变成七千五百万美元。俞院长说：在台湾绝对募不到这么多民间投资，必须先找一家「跨国」、有技术的IC公司，要他们做主要投资者；然后台湾民间才有信心凑足余额。

俞院长的第一指示是金玉良言，我完全接受。第二指示虽然令我失望，但他一定知道台湾民间的投资心态及投资胃纳，所以我也不得不接受。当然，邀请跨国、有技术的IC公司做主要投资者等于「引狼入室」，一定会带来「谁有控制权、经营权」问题。但是，当时第一要务是把公司办成，控制权、经营只好以后再见烦恼了。

见了俞院长后我就去李政委办公室，对他报告俞院长对我说的话，同时也告诉他我这几天听到关于陈主委的阻力：陈主委想找国外顾问公司评审我的「专业晶圆代工」公司建议，他又召集他的替代方案的座谈会，就在次日开会。

李政委对俞院长指示的两点倒没说什么，但对陈主委的阻挠行动却勃然大怒。他立刻命他秘书接电话给国科会副部长王纪五，在电话上对王怒吼：「告诉你的主管，他这样干涉我要做的事情，我要辞职了！」对陈要找国外顾问公司评审我的建议，李也气愤地对王说：「关于半导体问题，国外顾问公司是要请教张忠谋的，哪里有要他们评估张忠谋的道理。」李以「四朝重臣」之尊，暂时压倒了这次陈主委的阻力。当天我就接到「座谈会延期」的通知。几天后，我也间接被告知陈主委已不再阻挠。

十一月十七日（星期日），我访李政委于他家。看起来，俞院长对我的两指示都可遵守，陈主委也不再阻挠，我们应该请俞院长准许我们正式开始筹备工作。李政委回答：还是先见俞院长，看他有什么指示。

十一月二十二日，与李政委同见俞院长，我对俞院长报告新公司进行之目前状况，约半小时。俞院长简短回答：「写公文给我。」此后几天，我写我生平第一篇中文公文，也是我三十几年来第一篇中文作文。上次正式写中文是三十几年前写《伊莉莎伯》短篇小说。那次写中文小说的诗情画意，这次写公没有，有的只是硬邦邦台积电的雏型。

Philips' Investment and the Five-Person Committee

In early October — around the time Minister Li was worried about Premier Yu being "uncomfortable" after hearing Minister Chen's objections — Philips of the Netherlands approached Minister Li proactively: Philips was interested in investing in the new IC company plan they had read about in the newspapers. Philips was a diversified multinational with a semiconductor division and its own IC technology. So if their investment materialized, it would meet Premier Yu's funding requirement.

Upon hearing from Minister Li, I moved quickly on the Philips deal. I spent several days writing an investment proposal for Philips, delivered through Philips' technical manager in Taiwan to their headquarters. From November 3 to 6, I traveled to the Netherlands to visit Philips' two major sites: Nijmegen and Eindhoven. In mid-November, Philips reaffirmed their interest in a joint venture. Of course, many conditions and details remained to be negotiated, and such negotiations often take months, but I believed they were sincere.

On October 8, I met with Premier Yu. Yu handed me Minister Li's memorandum (recommending they proceed with TSMC as I had proposed) and asked me to "study it further." At the same time, he issued two directives: first, our proposed equity-to-loan ratio (50/50) was not conservative enough — it should be changed to 70 (equity) / 30 (loans). Second, with this change, the private investment needed became $75 million USD. Premier Yu said: This amount could absolutely not be raised from Taiwan's private sector; they had to find a "multinational," technology-bearing IC company to be the lead investor, and only then would Taiwan's private sector have confidence to raise the remainder.

Premier Yu's first directive was golden advice; I accepted it wholeheartedly. His second directive, though disappointing, reflected his knowledge of Taiwan's private investment appetite and mentality, so I had tooaccept it. Of course, inviting a multinational IC company to be the lead investor was tantamount to "inviting the wolf into the house" and would certainly raise "who controls and manages" issues. But at that moment, the first priority was to get the company founded; control and management could be worried about later.

After seeing Premier Yu, I went to Minister Li's office to report what Premier Yu had told me. I also informed him about Minister Chen's resistance: Chen wanted to engage a foreign consulting firm to evaluate my "dedicated foundry" proposal, and had convened a symposium on his alternative plan, scheduled for the next day.

Minister Li said little about Premier Yu's two directives, but he flew into a rage at Minister Chen's obstruction. He immediately ordered his secretary to call NSC Vice Minister Wang Jiwu, roaring at Wang on the phone: "Tell his superior that if he interferes with what I'm doing like this, I'll resign!" Regarding Chen's plan to have foreign consultants evaluate me, Li angrily told Wang: "On semiconductor matters, foreign consultants should be consulting Morris Chang — how could they possibly evaluate him?"

Li, leveraging his stature as a "four-dynasty elder statesman," temporarily crushed Minister Chen's resistance. That very day I received notice that the symposium was "postponed." A few days later, I was indirectly informed that Minister Chen was no longer obstructing.

On November 17 (Sunday), I visited Minister Li at his home. It appeared that Premier Yu's two directives could be followed, Minister Chen was no longer obstructing, and we should ask Premier Yu to authorize us to formally begin preparations. Minister Li responded: Let's still see Premier Yu first and see what he says.

On November 22, I accompanied Minister Li to see Premier Yu. I briefed Premier Yu on the current status of the new company for about half an hour. Premier Yu gave a brief answer: "Write me an official document."

In the following days, I wrote the first official document of my life — and my first piece of Chinese writing in over thirty years. The last time I had formally written in Chinese was more than thirty years earlier, writing the short story "Elizabeth." That time had been full of poetic sentiment; this time there was nothing romantic — only the hard, bare prototype of TSMC.

Cheat Sheet · 商业语汇
"Inviting the wolf into the house" (引狼入室)—Invite a wolf into the house — 比喻引来强大对手进入自己的地盘；张忠谋深知飞利浦作为主要投资者将带来控制权问题，但当时别无选择。
Four-dynasty elder statesman (四朝老臣)—指李国鼎历经蒋中正、严家淦、蒋经国、李登辉四朝均居要职的政治地位；李政委借此身份暂时压倒了陈履安的阻挠。
Official document (公文)—政府机关间正式的书面文件；张忠谋生平第一次写中文公文——距他上次正式写中文（短篇小说）已隔三十余年。

公文接力赛与正式批准

我还记得我把初稿给李政委看时，李政委频频摇头。他先告诉我要采取的格式，等我再次写稿后又仔细帮我修改字句，又告诉我以工研院院长身份，不应直接写签呈给俞院长，而应签呈给经济部部长李达海。我忙了几天后，于十一月二十七日签呈李达海部长，重点如下：

（一）共需资本两亿零两百万美元，七〇%投资（Equity），三〇%贷款。

（二）投资（Equity）部分一亿四千五百万美元。股份分配计划如下：政府七千万美元（四八．三%）；其他国内或国外投资三千五百万美元（二四．一%）；飞利浦投资可能性甚高。

（三）今日建立TSMC之原因，至少有四。

（四）总经理人选应为已在国际VLSI工业有相当管理地位、熟识最新制造技术、且能与国外市场建立密切关系者。大约需一美国人。需在美国招雇人员约十人左右。中下级干部人员可在台湾招雇，电子所可移转约一百名工程人员，应足够初步需要。

李达海部长接到我的签呈后又等了一个月，直至十二月三十日才签呈俞院长，除了摘述我对他的签呈外，他加了：「拟请钧院核定后指定有关首长成立筹划指导小组协调筹划及诱导资金必需租税措施，并请工研院张院长为执行秘书兼办筹建工作。」此后行政院的行动就快了。（一九八六年）一月四日，行政院秘书长王章清函经建会：请经建会「提前审议」台积电；一月八日经建会就开会，主席为主委赵耀东，副主席为主委王昭明，我记得的出席委员有财政部部长钱纯、经济部部长李达海、交通部部长连战、中央银行总裁张继正。我又报告了一次新创的「专业代工」模式，以及我十一月二十七日签呈李部长的重点。报告后赵主委征求各委员意见，最令我难忘的是张继正总裁与我的对白：

张总裁：「你凭什么与美、日、韩公司竞争？」我：「我们专业做晶圆代工，我凭好的服务竞争。」张总裁哈哈了一声：「哈，台湾公司要凭商誉竞争，倒是第一次听闻。」我那时虽听懂这是讥讽性的评语，但不太懂：难道台湾公司从不讲商誉？幸而没有别的委员借张总裁之题发挥。张总裁的话也像风一样，过了就没有了。

次日，赵主委就发文行政院秘书长：原则同意进行本案，并同意成立筹划指导小组，并请工研院张院长忠谋为执行秘书，兼办筹建工作。

一月十六日，行政院院会决定接受经建会的结论。一月二十八日，俞院长行文经济部等五部会及工研院，指派赵耀东主委、李达海部长为筹划指导小组的共同召集人；钱纯财政部部长、陈履安主委及我为小组成员，我也是执行秘书。这就是所谓「五人小组」。

促成台积电最出力的李政委，却不在「五人小组」内。李政委对我说，他自己要求俞院长不在小组内；又说，他功成身退了一九八五年九月十日我对俞院长简报、首次倡议台积电，到次年一月二十八日俞院长指定「筹划指导」五人小组，可说是筹备台积电的第一幕；第二幕即将展开。
